summarize_spoken_text.title: The value of failure
summarize_spoken_text.transcript: Many students are terrified of failure. They choose easy courses, avoid difficult questions, and see every low mark as a judgment on their intelligence. But research on learning tells a different story. When we struggle with a problem and get it wrong, our brains are forced to work harder, and that effort makes the eventual solution far more memorable. Psychologists call this productive failure. In one well-known study, students who attempted complex maths problems before being taught the method outperformed those who were shown the method first. The key, though, is that failure must be followed by feedback and reflection. Simply failing repeatedly without understanding why does not help. So my advice is to treat mistakes as information, not as a verdict.

key_points.label: students fear failure and avoid challenges
struggling and failing makes learning more memorable
productive failure: study where trying first outperformed being taught first
failure must be followed by feedback and reflection

summarize_spoken_text.title: Light pollution
summarize_spoken_text.transcript: When we think of pollution, we usually imagine dirty air or plastic in the ocean. But light can also be a pollutant. Artificial lighting at night has grown so much that, in many cities, it is impossible to see more than a handful of stars. This matters for more than astronomy. Many animals rely on natural darkness: migrating birds use the stars to navigate, and baby sea turtles find the ocean by moving towards the brightest horizon, which, near coastal towns, is often a road rather than the sea. Humans are affected too. Exposure to bright light at night disrupts the production of melatonin, a hormone that regulates sleep. Fortunately, light pollution is one of the easiest kinds to fix. Shielding street lights so they point downwards, using warmer colours and switching off unnecessary lights can make an immediate difference.

key_points.label: artificial light at night is a form of pollution hiding the stars
it harms animals such as birds and sea turtles
it disrupts human sleep via melatonin
it is easy to fix: shielding, warmer lights, switching off

mcq_multiple_listening.title: Supermarket psychology
mcq_multiple_listening.transcript: Supermarkets are carefully designed to encourage us to spend more. Essential items like bread and milk are usually placed at the back of the store, so customers must walk past many other products to reach them. The most profitable goods are displayed at eye level, while cheaper alternatives are placed on lower shelves. Some stores even play slow music, because research shows that shoppers move more slowly and buy more when the tempo is relaxed. Being aware of these techniques, and shopping with a list, can help consumers resist impulse purchases.
mcq_multiple_listening.question: Which strategies used by supermarkets are mentioned?

options.text: Placing essential items at the back of the store
Offering free samples at the entrance
Putting profitable products at eye level

mcq_multiple_listening.title: Sleep and teenagers
mcq_multiple_listening.transcript: Teenagers are often criticised for staying up late and sleeping in, but biology is partly to blame. During adolescence, the body releases melatonin later in the evening, which shifts the natural sleep cycle by up to two hours. Several school districts that moved their start times later reported better attendance, fewer car accidents among teenage drivers, and modest improvements in grades. Critics point out, however, that later start times can create problems for parents' work schedules and for after-school sports.
mcq_multiple_listening.question: According to the speaker, which outcomes were reported after schools started later?

options.text: Fewer car accidents involving teenage drivers

highlight_correct_summary.title: Why we procrastinate
highlight_correct_summary.transcript: We often assume that procrastination is a problem of laziness or poor time management. However, psychologists increasingly see it as a problem of emotion regulation. When a task makes us feel anxious, bored or insecure, putting it off provides immediate relief from those negative feelings. Unfortunately, that relief is temporary, and the stress returns, usually stronger, as the deadline approaches. Strategies that address the emotions, such as breaking the task into small steps or being kind to ourselves about past delays, tend to work better than simply making stricter schedules.

options.text: Procrastination is mainly caused by laziness, so stricter schedules are the best solution.
Procrastination is a way of avoiding negative emotions linked to a task, and strategies that address those emotions are more effective than strict scheduling.
Procrastination reduces stress in the long term because it gives people time to relax before a deadline.
Psychologists believe procrastination cannot be overcome and should therefore be accepted.

highlight_correct_summary.title: Urban trees
highlight_correct_summary.transcript: City trees do far more than make streets look pleasant. They provide shade that can lower surface temperatures by several degrees, absorb rainwater that would otherwise overwhelm drainage systems, and filter some pollutants from the air. Studies have also linked access to green space with lower stress. Despite this, many cities lose trees faster than they plant them, often because young trees are not watered or protected during their first few years.

options.text: Urban trees are mainly decorative, and cities should focus on planting more flowers instead.
Trees cool cities, reduce flooding, clean the air and benefit wellbeing, yet many cities lose trees because young ones are not cared for.
Most cities now plant more trees than they lose, thanks to better watering programmes.
Trees increase surface temperatures and put pressure on drainage systems in cities.

mcq_single_listening.title: Museum funding
mcq_single_listening.transcript: Our museum has always offered free entry, and we're proud of that. But public funding has fallen by almost a third over the past five years. Rather than introduce an entrance fee, which we believe would discourage families and students, we've decided to expand our café and gift shop, and to rent our galleries for private events in the evenings.

highlight_incorrect_words.transcript: The human body contains trillions of microorganisms, most of which live in the gut.
